Where it began

Sarfaraz Ahmed was born in Karachi on 22 May 1987, into a family that ran a printing business. He showed early that he could lead. In 2006 he captained Pakistan at the Under-19 World Cup and beat India in a low-scoring final to bring the trophy home.

His first chance for the senior side came in 2007 as cover for Kamran Akmal in a one-day series in India. He made his debut in the final match and did not get to bat, because Pakistan had already won. It was a quiet start to a career that would not stay quiet for long.

The player

He first kept wicket in a Test at Hobart in January 2010. Between then and 2023 he played 54 Tests, scoring 3,031 runs at 37.42 with four hundreds and 21 fifties, the best of them 118. Behind the stumps he held 159 catches and made 22 stumpings.

His innings of 96 from 85 balls at Galle in 2015 won him the man of the match award and took him past 1,000 Test runs, as fast as any Pakistani keeper had got there. At the 2015 World Cup he equalled the one-day record with six catches in an innings against South Africa, then made an unbeaten 101 against Ireland to take Pakistan into the quarter-finals.

What made him special

He was a natural captain, and Pakistan made him one in every format. In 2017 his side beat England in the Champions Trophy semi-final and then India in the final by 180 runs. He was picked as captain and keeper of the team of the tournament. His Twenty20 side won 11 series in a row and rose to number one in the world rankings. In Tests he led Pakistan 13 times, winning four.

His bat was always useful and often busy. If there was one gap in his game, it was that his hundreds came along less often than his fifties: 21 of those to four of the bigger ones. Nobody in Karachi was complaining.

Away from the middle

He captained Quetta Gladiators from the first season of the Pakistan Super League. After two lost finals, they won the title in its fourth season. He received the Sitara-e-Imtiaz, one of Pakistan's highest civilian awards, in 2018, and the board's spirit of cricket award the same year.

He announced his retirement from international cricket in March 2026. By then he was already looking after Pakistan's young players: the board put him in charge of the Shaheens and the Under-19 side in November 2025, and that team won the 2025 Under-19 Asia Cup. For the Test tour of Bangladesh in April 2026 he took charge of the national side as head coach.

And finally

His story has a neat shape to it. He began by leading Pakistan's boys to an Under-19 world title, and two decades later he was helping the next lot of boys win a trophy of their own.
